title: Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade: 2026 update
summary: Global trade in 2025 grew faster than the global economy despite tariff disruptions, with AI-related goods driving one-third of trade growth and emerging economies capturing significant market share. The United States and China experienced a 30 percent decline in bilateral trade due to tariffs, but this gap was largely filled by ASEAN, India, and other geopolitically aligned trading partners. Trade increasingly reorganizes along geopolitical lines rather than pure economic efficiency, with durable structural shifts driven by AI, emerging market growth, and China's shift toward supplying manufacturing hubs rather than end-consumer goods.
central_argument: Geopolitical realignment is durably reshaping global trade patterns away from distant partners toward geopolitically aligned economies, even as tariffs and AI create new growth engines.
key_claims: AI-related trade (semiconductors, data center equipment) accounted for one-third of global trade growth in 2025
US–China bilateral trade fell by approximately 30 percent due to tariffs
The United States replaced about two-thirds of the tariff-induced import gap with goods from other sellers
Chinese exporters cut prices by an average of 8 percent to find buyers in new markets
ASEAN increased trade with both the United States and China simultaneously
Trade grew faster than global output in 2025 despite dire predictions of retrenchment
China expanded its role as a 'factory to the factories' by increasing exports of industrial components and capital goods to emerging economies
key_tensions: Trade reorientation toward geopolitically aligned partners contradicts predictions of trade collapse under tariff regimes
Tariff-driven disruptions coexist with structural growth in AI-related trade and emerging market manufacturing
The European Union faced a double squeeze from both Chinese imports and US tariffs while other regions thrived
